title: The Effects of Class Size on Student Achievement: New Evidence from Population Variation
research_question: Does reducing class size in elementary grades improve student academic achievement, and do any such effects differ across schools serving low-income or minority student populations?
data_description: The study uses a longitudinal panel of 649 elementary schools in 146 elementary districts in Connecticut. Enrollment data span 24 years (allowing estimation of school-grade-specific trends), district-level test data span 1986-87 through 1997-98 (12 years), and school-level test data span 1992-93 through 1997-98 (6 years). Connecticut administered statewide standardized tests in math, reading, and writing at the start of grades 4, 6, and 8. Key variables include grade-level enrollment, average class size (mean ~21, sd ~5.5), district-level kindergarten-age population counts (from Enumerations of Children and Claritas), district maximum and minimum class size rules collected via a survey of superintendents, and district demographic controls from the 1990 Census (median household income, poverty rate, educational attainment, racial composition). Test scores are normalized by the standard deviation of school-level scores. The unit of observation is a school-grade-cohort (or district-grade-cohort).
institutional_context: Class size reduction is among the most popular and heavily funded U.S. school improvement policies, exemplified by California's 1996 $1 billion-per-year initiative and a 1999 federal $12 billion (seven-year) program. Elementary schools are an apt setting because instruction is typically delivered by a single teacher per classroom, making class size well-defined, and because the integer nature of classrooms translates population fluctuations directly into class-size variation. Connecticut is well-suited because towns serve as school districts, long histories of annual child enumerations are available, and districts maintain stable maximum and minimum class size rules (modal maximum 25, modal minimum 15) that were largely set in the early 1980s. When grade enrollment crosses these thresholds, schools must add or remove a classroom, generating sharp jumps in class size. Idiosyncratic year-to-year fluctuations in birth timing also produce naturally varying cohort sizes within schools.
